summary: Defines Megaco, a protocol used between a Media Gateway and a Media Gateway Controller when a telephony gateway is split into those two parts. The controller makes decisions and the gateway moves the media. It is the same protocol as ITU-T H.248. It was replaced by RFC 3525.

plainLanguage.summary: Picture a phone switch split into a brain that decides and hands that do the work. This is the language the brain uses to tell the hands what to do. A newer version later replaced it.

questions: protocol between media gateway and controller
what is the difference between megaco and h.248
what is a media gateway controller
subtitle: How a telephony gateway's decision-making brain talks to its media-moving hands, as defined for Megaco and ITU-T H.248.

tldr.problem: A multimedia gateway can be split into a Media Gateway that handles the media and a Media Gateway Controller that makes the decisions, and the two parts need a common language to work together.
tldr.mechanism: The protocol models the gateway as Terminations joined into Contexts, and the controller manipulates them with eight commands (Add, Modify, Subtract, Move, AuditValue, AuditCapabilities, Notify, ServiceChange) grouped into Transactions.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3015 was obsoleted by RFC 3525, which is the current version of the Megaco protocol. It is common text with ITU-T Recommendation H.248.

today: RFC 3015 has been obsoleted by RFC 3525, which is the current version of the Megaco protocol, so new work should follow that document. RFC 3015 itself obsoleted RFC 2885 and RFC 2886 and is a Proposed Standard published in November 2000.

sections.title: Scope and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 3015 defines the protocol used between the elements of a physically decomposed multimedia gateway: a Media Gateway (MG) and a Media Gateway Controller (MGC). The MG converts media from one type of network to the format required by another, for example by terminating circuit-switched channels and packet-network media streams. The MGC controls the parts of the call state that concern connection control for media channels in the MG.

The RFC says that from a system view there is no functional difference between such a decomposed gateway and a monolithic one. It does not define how gateways, multipoint control units or interactive voice response units work. Instead it creates a general framework that is suitable for them.

The text is common with ITU-T Recommendation H.248 and is the result of applying the changes in RFC 2886 to the text of RFC 2885. It meets the requirements for a media gateway control protocol given in RFC 2805.
sections.plainLanguage: A big phone machine can be split in two: one part that thinks and one part that moves the sound around. This document is the language they use to talk to each other.

sections.title: The Connection Model: Terminations and Contexts
sections.content:
The protocol describes the logical objects inside the MG that the MGC can control. There are two main abstractions. A Termination sources and/or sinks one or more media or control streams, and it holds the media stream, modem and bearer parameters. A Context is an association between a collection of Terminations. It describes the topology (who hears or sees whom) and the mixing or switching parameters when more than two Terminations are involved.

A special null Context holds all Terminations that are not associated with any other Termination. In a decomposed access gateway, idle lines sit there. A Termination exists in only one Context at a time. Contexts are created implicitly when a Termination is added without naming an existing one, and deleted implicitly when the last Termination leaves.

Terminations for physical things, such as a TDM channel, have a semi-permanent existence. Ephemeral ones, such as RTP flows, exist only while used and are created by Add and destroyed by Subtract. Each Termination has a TerminationID chosen by the MG. Two wildcards can be used in a TerminationID: ALL addresses many Terminations at once, and CHOOSE asks the MG to pick one that fits a partial specification. A reserved Root TerminationID refers to the whole gateway.

The RFC illustrates the model with a call-waiting scenario: Termination T1 moves from Context C1 to Context C2 when it answers the waiting call from T3, leaving T2 on hold.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a Termination as one phone line or one sound stream, and a Context as a room where some of them are connected so they can talk. Lines that are not in a call wait in a special empty room.

sections.title: Packages and Registration
sections.content:
Different gateways have different kinds of Terminations. The protocol handles this with Packages: groups of optional Properties, Events, Signals and Statistics that a Termination can realize. The MGC can audit a Termination to see which Packages it supports. Items in a Package are named by the PackageID and the item ID, and in the text encoding they are separated by a slash, for example togen/playtone.

A Package description states its name, PackageID, description and version, an integer from 1 to 99. A new version can only add things; no deletions or modifications are allowed. A Package may also extend another one, but must not redefine a name from it. Packages defined by the IETF appear in separate RFCs.

For IANA, a package is registered with a unique string name (used in the text encoding), a serial number (used in the binary encoding), and a version. Serial numbers 60000 to 64565 are reserved for private use and serial number 0 is reserved. Packages registered by bodies other than recognized standards bodies need a name of at least 8 characters. Error codes and ServiceChange reasons have their own IANA registration rules. Annex E defines a set of basic packages, such as tone generation and detection, DTMF, RTP and TDM circuit packages.
sections.plainLanguage: Packages are like add-on toolkits. A basic gateway knows the basics, and each toolkit adds extra abilities, like making a dial tone. The controller can ask which toolkits a line has.

sections.title: Descriptors: The Parameters of Commands
sections.content:
Command parameters are grouped into Descriptors, each with a name and a list of items. The main ones are:

  • Media (with TerminationState and one or more Stream descriptors), Modem and Mux, for the media, modem and multiplex settings of a Termination.
  • LocalControl, Local and Remote inside a Stream. Local describes media the MG receives and Remote describes media it sends. In the text encoding these use SDP session descriptions (RFC 2327), with a few relaxations such as optional s=, t= and o= lines.
  • Events and EventBuffer, for what the MG should detect and report, and Signals, for tones or announcements it should play.
  • DigitMap, Statistics, Packages, ObservedEvents, Audit and ServiceChange.

Parameters may be fully specified, under-specified with CHOOSE so the responder picks a value, or over-specified with a list in order of preference. The MG returns the value it chose. The LocalControl descriptor has a Mode (send-only, receive-only, send/receive, inactive, loop-back) and the Reserve properties ReserveValue and ReserveGroup, which default to false and control whether the MG reserves resources for all offered alternatives or commits to one.

A digit map is a dialing plan held in the MG, used to report a group of digit events together instead of one by one. It can be matched with a start timer (T), short timer (S) and long timer (L). A Topology descriptor, optional to implement, sets who receives media from whom inside a Context, using the associations isolate, oneway and bothway. The default is that each Termination is received by all others.
sections.plainLanguage: A descriptor is like a form the controller fills in. One form says what sound settings to use, another says what to watch for, like someone picking up the phone, and another says what tone to play.

sections.title: The Eight Commands
sections.content:
Most commands go from the MGC to the MG. The exceptions are Notify, which goes from MG to MGC, and ServiceChange, which either side may send.

  • Add adds a Termination to a Context; adding the first one creates the Context. Add must not be used on a Termination whose serviceState is OutofService.
  • Modify changes properties, events and signals of a Termination.
  • Subtract removes a Termination from its Context and returns statistics. Subtracting the last one deletes the Context.
  • Move atomically moves a Termination to another Context. It cannot be used to move to or from the null Context.
  • AuditValue and AuditCapabilities return current state and the possible values the MG allows.
  • Notify reports detected events, with a RequestID that links it to the Events descriptor that asked for it.
  • ServiceChange announces that Terminations are going out of or back into service, and is also how an MG registers with an MGC.

ServiceChange has a method: Graceful, Forced, Restart, Disconnected, Handoff or Failover (or a value both sides understand). A ServiceChange with the Root TerminationID and method Restart is a registration command by which an MG announces itself. The reason is an IANA-registered code from 900 (Service Restored) to 915 (State Loss).
sections.plainLanguage: The controller has a small set of orders: put a line in a call, change a line, take it out, move it, ask how it is doing, and so on. The gateway can also tap the controller on the shoulder to say something happened.

sections.title: Error Codes
sections.content:
An error is reported in an error descriptor made of an IANA-registered code and an optional explanatory string. Implementations are encouraged to append diagnostic information to the string. The codes fall into groups by their first digit: 4xx for request and syntax problems, such as 400 Bad Request, 403 Syntax Error in Transaction, 406 Version Not Supported, 430 Unknown TerminationID and 440 Unsupported or unknown Package; and 5xx for gateway-side problems, such as 500 Internal Gateway Error, 501 Not Implemented, 505 Command Received before Restart Response and 510 Insufficient resources.

Section 8 specifies which error to return when parsing fails. If a legal Action cannot be determined, the reply is 422 Syntax Error in Action. If a legal Transaction cannot be determined, the reply carries a null TransactionID and 403. If a command's end or TerminationID cannot be determined, the reply is 442 Syntax Error in Command.
sections.plainLanguage: When something goes wrong, the gateway sends back a number and a short note saying what the problem was, like a teacher writing a reason next to a mark.

sections.title: Transactions, Actions and Messages
sections.content:
Commands are grouped into Transactions, each identified by a TransactionID assigned by the sender. A Transaction contains one or more Actions, and each Action is a series of Commands limited to a single Context. Several Transactions can be concatenated into a Message. The message header carries the sender identity (MID) and a version number, which starts at 1.

Commands within a Transaction run in order; Transactions themselves are not ordered and may run in any order or at once. Processing stops at the first failing Command, unless the command is marked Optional. If a command fails, the MG should as far as possible restore the state from before it. A TransactionReply holds the results, and a TransactionPending tells the sender the work is still in progress, so it does not assume the request was lost.

The protocol can be encoded in binary, defined with ASN.1 in Annex A, or in text, defined with ABNF (RFC 2234) in Annex B. MGCs should support both encodings; MGs may support both.
sections.plainLanguage: A transaction is like one envelope containing a to-do list. The gateway does the list in order, stops if one item cannot be done, and sends back a single answer. If the job is slow it says "still working on it".

sections.title: Registration, Failover and Restart
sections.content:
An MG is pre-provisioned with a primary MGC and optionally an ordered list of secondary ones. On a cold start it sends a ServiceChange with method Restart on the Root Termination to its primary MGC. The MGC may answer with a different ServiceChangeMgcId, in which case the MG contacts that controller. If nobody replies, the MG tries its secondaries in order, and if all fail it waits a random time and starts again. If a command arrives before the Restart response, the MG answers with error 505.

The first ServiceChange from an MG carries its protocol version in ServiceChangeVersion. If the MGC supports only a lower version, both sides use the lower version; if they cannot agree, the association is rejected with error 406. The RFC also gives rules for extending the protocol: existing elements should not change meaning, and obsolete ones are marked as reserved so identifiers are not reused.

To avoid a restart avalanche when many gateways power on at once, each MG should wait a random time, uniformly distributed between 0 and a maximum waiting delay (MWD), before restarting. Residential gateways without explicit configuration should use 600 seconds for MWD. For trunking gateways the RFC gives 2.5 seconds for a T1 line and 60 milliseconds for a T3 line as examples.

A failed MG may send ServiceChange with method Forced or Graceful, and a failover to a backup uses method Failover. An MGC can hand its MGs to a replacement using the Handoff method. A physical MG may also be split into virtual MGs, each with its own Root Termination and its own controller.
sections.plainLanguage: When a gateway wakes up it knocks on its controller's door. If the controller is away, it tries the backup, and to stop every gateway from knocking at the same second, each waits a random moment first.

sections.title: Transport over UDP and TCP
sections.content:
The transport should allow reliable delivery of transactions and must not depend on which commands are sent. For IP, MGCs shall implement both TCP and UDP with Application Level Framing (UDP/ALF), and an MG shall implement TCP or UDP/ALF or both. The default port is 2944 for text-encoded and 2945 for binary-encoded operation, over either UDP or TCP. Replies go back to the address the request came from, even if a ServiceChangeAddress was given for later requests.

Over UDP, most commands are not idempotent, so the RFC requires at-most-once behavior. Each side keeps a list of recent responses and outstanding transactions, and answers a duplicate with the saved response instead of executing it again. Transaction identifiers are 32-bit integers. A suggested value for the LONG-TIMER used to hold these records is 30 seconds. Retransmission timers are not fixed but must back off exponentially. The RFC notes a TCP-style estimate with a suggested maximum of 4 seconds and describes a Transaction Pending provisional response. Once more than T-MAX has elapsed with no answer, the MG concludes the MGC has failed and recovers with a ServiceChange using the Disconnected method.

Over TCP, which carries a byte stream, TPKT as in RFC 1006 must be used to mark message boundaries. Commands are not guaranteed to arrive in order across transactions, so section 9.1 gives rules for MGCs, such as keeping at most one outstanding Add, Modify or Move per Termination.
sections.plainLanguage: Because a letter might get lost, the sender keeps resending until it hears back. The receiver keeps notes so that if the same letter arrives twice it only does the job once.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The protocol can set up calls, so unauthorized use must be prevented. Over IP, the security mechanism is IPsec. The AH header (RFC 2402) gives data origin authentication, connectionless integrity and optional anti-replay protection, and ESP (RFC 2406) gives confidentiality. Implementations SHOULD use IKE for more robust keying.

Because AH or ESP is inserted right after the IP header, which is hard to do at the application level, the RFC defines an optional interim AH scheme inside the protocol header, using the SPI, sequence number and data fields of RFC 2402. Implementations using IPv4 SHALL implement it, but it SHALL NOT be used when the network layer supports IPsec, and IPv6 implementations SHALL NOT use it. The scheme does not protect against eavesdropping or replay attacks.

The RFC also discusses "uncontrolled barge-in", where an attacker sends media packets to the address and port of a connection. Checking the source address helps but slows setup and can be fooled by spoofing. An alternative is to encrypt and authenticate the media using a secret key conveyed during call setup.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone who sneaks in could make calls or listen to them. So messages are sealed and signed, and the media can be locked with a secret key so only the right people can use it.

root.label: Message
root.note: header with sender MID and version

items.label: Add
items.desc: Adds a Termination to a Context; the first one creates the Context.

items.label: Modify
items.desc: Changes properties, events and signals of a Termination.

items.label: Subtract
items.desc: Removes a Termination from its Context and returns statistics.

items.label: Move
items.desc: Atomically moves a Termination to another Context.

items.label: AuditValue
items.desc: Returns current properties, events, signals and statistics.

items.label: AuditCapabilities
items.desc: Returns all possible values the MG allows.

items.label: Notify
items.desc: MG tells the MGC that events occurred.

items.label: ServiceChange
items.desc: Announces Terminations going in or out of service, and MG registration.

viz.caption: MG REGISTRATION, SIMPLIFIED FROM THE RFC EXAMPLE

messages.label: ServiceChange (Root, Restart)
messages.note: The MG announces itself; this must be the first message the MGC sees from it.

messages.label: Reply
messages.note: Acknowledgement completes registration unless the MGC names another controller.

items.label: Graceful
items.desc: Terminations go out of service after the delay; existing connections are not yet affected.

items.label: Forced
items.desc: Terminations were taken abruptly out of service and connections were lost.

items.label: Restart
items.desc: Service will be restored after the delay; at Root it is a registration.

items.label: Disconnected
items.desc: The MG lost contact with its MGC and it was later restored.

items.label: Handoff
items.desc: The MGC is going out of service and a new association must be set up.

items.label: Failover
items.desc: Sent by the MG to indicate a primary is out of service and a secondary takes over.
